Characteristics of Specific Aquifers
Alluvium and Colluvium - Alluvium underlies the valleys of Sarpy and East Fork Sarpy Creek, and colluvium covers the sides of the lower slopes of the valleys. The alluvium is from 30 to 80 feet thick (Westmoreland Resources, 1975 k, p. 15) and consists of loosely compacted, angular to sub-rounded, moderate to poorly uniform deposits of gravel, sand, silt, and lesser amounts of clay. There is usually a zone of low permeability about five feet below the organic soil horizon (Westmoreland Resources 1975 1, p. 29). Water occurs in the voids between the soil grains of the alluvium. Recharge is by precipitation, and from springs, and lateral flow through the bedrock on the flanks of the valleys. In the winter and spring, water is transmitted from the flanks of the valleys, through the alluvium and discharges in the creeks. In summer and fall, flow in the creeks recharges the alluvium. Some water may also move vertically through the alluvium to recharge deeper aquifers. In summer, water levels in the alluvium are 15 to 25 feet below land surface, which is below the base of nearby stream channels (Westmoreland Resouces, 1975 1, p. 26).
Pumping tests of wells in alluvium indicated a yield of from 5 to 40 gpm, transmissivities of from 1000 to 12,000 gpd/ft and permeabilities of from 1 x 10<sup>-3</sup> to 1 x 10 2 cm/sec. Calculations of underflow in the alluvium were made using a permeability of 5 x 10<sup>-3</sup> cm/sec. A flow of 30 gpm for Sarpy Creek and 40 gpm for East Fork Sarpy Creek was indicated. (Westmoreland Resources, 1975 1, p. 27 and 28).
